scenes.tts: How does your ear know whether a tone is high or low?
scenes.visual: A high note and a low note shown as two waveforms. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: How does your ear know whether a tone is high or low?

scenes.tts: Uncoil the cochlea. Along it runs the basilar membrane, carrying the hair cells.
scenes.visual: The cochlea's coil unrolls into a straight tube. A long membrane runs along it with a row of hair cells.
scenes.narration: Uncoil the cochlea. Along it runs the basilar membrane, carrying the hair cells.

scenes.tts: Near the base, where sound enters, it is narrow and stiff. Toward the apex it is wide and floppy.
scenes.visual: The membrane drawn narrow at the base end, widening toward the apex. Labels: base, narrow and stiff; apex, wide and floppy.
scenes.narration: Near the base, where sound enters, it is narrow and stiff. Toward the apex it is wide and floppy.

scenes.tts: So each place has a natural frequency, high where the membrane is stiff, low where it is floppy.
scenes.visual: A colour gradient along the membrane, labelled high natural frequency at the base and low at the apex.
scenes.narration: So each place has a natural frequency, high where the membrane is stiff, low where it is floppy.

scenes.tts: Sound sets up a travelling wave that moves from the base toward the apex.
scenes.visual: A ripple starts at the base and travels along the membrane.
scenes.narration: Sound sets up a travelling wave that moves from the base toward the apex.

scenes.tts: A high tone's wave slows and grows near its matching place, close to the base.
scenes.visual: A high tone's wave slows and grows a short way from the base.
scenes.narration: A high tone's wave slows and grows near its matching place, close to the base.

scenes.tts: It peaks there, then dies away.
scenes.visual: The wave's envelope peaks near the base and falls to nothing just beyond. Hair cells under the peak light up.
scenes.narration: It peaks there, then dies away.

scenes.tts: Now a low tone enters at the same base. Where will its wave peak?
scenes.visual: A second, slower waveform enters at the base. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Now a low tone enters at the same base. Where will its wave peak?

scenes.tts: Near the apex, where the membrane is floppy and its natural frequency is low.
scenes.visual: The low tone's wave travels past the base and peaks near the apex. Hair cells there light up.
scenes.narration: Near the apex, where the membrane is floppy and its natural frequency is low.

scenes.tts: Frequency becomes position. This map is called tonotopy.
scenes.visual: Both peaks shown together on the membrane. Label: frequency becomes position (tonotopy).
scenes.narration: Frequency becomes position. This map is called tonotopy.

scenes.tts: Above about one kilohertz, each doubling of frequency takes nearly the same length of membrane.
scenes.caption: Above about 1 kHz, each doubling of frequency takes nearly the same length of membrane.
scenes.visual: A ruler along the membrane labelled: Greenwood map, human cochlea, 35 mm assumed. Octave marks at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 kHz sit 14.0, 18.6, 23.3, 28.2 and 33.2 mm from the apex, about 5 mm apart. Then marks for 62, 125, 250 and 500 Hz appear, closer and closer together toward the apex.
scenes.narration: Above about 1 kHz, each doubling of frequency takes nearly the same length of membrane.

scenes.tts: Georg von Baykayshee measured these waves. His peaks were far broader than a living ear's tuning.
scenes.caption: Georg von Békésy measured these waves. His peaks were far broader than a living ear's tuning.
scenes.visual: Name on screen: Georg von Békésy, 1961 Nobel Prize. His broad envelope overlaid on a living ear's sharp, narrow peak.
scenes.narration: Georg von Békésy measured these waves. His peaks were far broader than a living ear's tuning.

scenes.tts: Something in a living ear adds energy. That something is the outer hair cells.
scenes.visual: Cross-section: one row of inner hair cells and three rows of outer hair cells on the membrane; the outer rows highlighted.
scenes.narration: Something in a living ear adds energy. That something is the outer hair cells.

scenes.tts: They change length when their voltage changes. The motor is a membrane protein called prestin.
scenes.visual: An outer hair cell lengthens and shortens. Labels: electromotility; prestin, driven by voltage, not ATP.
scenes.narration: They change length when their voltage changes. The motor is a membrane protein called prestin.

scenes.tts: Each outer hair cell is braced between the basilar membrane and the structures above it.
scenes.visual: An outer hair cell standing between the basilar membrane below and the structures above it; as the cell shortens and lengthens, the membrane moves with it.
scenes.narration: Each outer hair cell is braced between the basilar membrane and the structures above it.

scenes.tts: Here is the loop. The membrane moves, and an outer hair cell's bundle is pushed.
scenes.visual: Loop diagram, step one: membrane moves, bundle pushed.
scenes.narration: Here is the loop. The membrane moves, and an outer hair cell's bundle is pushed.

scenes.tts: Its voltage swings, and prestin shortens and lengthens the cell.
scenes.visual: Loop steps two and three: voltage swings; prestin changes the cell's length.
scenes.narration: Its voltage swings, and prestin shortens and lengthens the cell.

scenes.tts: Its push is timed to go with the membrane's motion, like pushing a swing. That adds energy near the peak.
scenes.visual: Loop step four: a force arrow on the membrane always points the way the membrane is moving, like a hand pushing a swing along; the peak grows taller and sharper.
scenes.narration: Its push is timed to go with the membrane's motion, like pushing a swing. That adds energy near the peak.

scenes.tts: The same switch, used as a motor. It sharpens tuning and raises sensitivity.
scenes.visual: Label: the same switch, used as a motor. Sharper tuning, more sensitivity.
scenes.narration: The same switch, used as a motor. It sharpens tuning and raises sensitivity.

scenes.tts: The boost is largest for quiet sounds. Lose the outer hair cells, and the threshold of hearing rises: quiet sounds drop below it.
scenes.visual: Two bars: a quiet tone boosted a lot, a loud tone boosted little. A dashed line, labelled illustrative detection threshold for this tone, marks the threshold of hearing. The outer hair cells fade out; the quiet tone's peak shrinks and broadens and falls below the line, but does not vanish.
scenes.narration: The boost is largest for quiet sounds. Lose the outer hair cells, and the threshold of hearing rises: quiet sounds drop below it.

scenes.tts: If the inner hair cells and their nerve fibres still work, sounds above the new threshold are still heard. But tuning blurs.
scenes.visual: The loud tone's peak stays above the threshold line, but broad.
scenes.narration: If the inner hair cells and their nerve fibres still work, sounds above the new threshold are still heard. But tuning blurs.

scenes.tts: Inner hair cells supply most of the auditory nerve. They report the place.
scenes.visual: The inner hair cell row highlighted, with most nerve fibres drawn from it.
scenes.narration: Inner hair cells supply most of the auditory nerve. They report the place.

scenes.tts: The brain reads pitch from where the active cells are.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the wave decides which bundles are pushed; the brain reads pitch from where the active cells are.
scenes.narration: The brain reads pitch from where the active cells are.
